meta.name: CompTIA SecurityX (CAS-005)
meta.notes: Initial CAS-005 SecurityX pack (formerly CASP+); covers GRC, security architecture, engineering and operations. | v1.1 (2026-07-03): +10 scenario questions — continuous adaptive access, post-quantum/crypto-agility, SAST/DAST/SCA pipeline, SASE, merger segmentation, order of volatility, API rate limiting, HSM key protection, MITRE ATT&CK hunting, tokenization/masking. Rebalanced correct positions (was 50% top slot).

questions.question: A multinational firm is consolidating identity onto a single cloud IdP and wants every workforce login, including for legacy on-prem apps that only speak Kerberos or header-based auth, to be brokered through that IdP with conditional access and continuous evaluation. Which architectural pattern fits best?
options: Deploy an identity-aware proxy (IAP) in front of the legacy apps and federate the IdP via SAML/OIDC to the proxy
Synchronise password hashes from the IdP into the legacy directories so each app authenticates locally
Publish the legacy apps to the internet behind a CDN-based WAF with IP allow-listing for corporate ranges
Distribute long-lived service-account credentials to users and rotate them via a password vault
questions.explanation: An identity-aware proxy sits in front of the legacy app and terminates the user session with the modern IdP over SAML/OIDC, then injects the Kerberos ticket or auth header downstream. This brings the legacy app under conditional access and continuous evaluation without rewriting it. Synchronising hashes leaves each app authenticating locally and bypasses central policy, a WAF with allow-listing enforces network rules but not user identity, and shared service accounts violate non-repudiation.

questions.question: An architect is asked to make the firm "crypto-agile" ahead of NIST's post-quantum migration. Which design choice most directly enables a future swap from RSA-2048 to a PQC algorithm like ML-KEM without re-architecting applications?
options: Pin a single cipher suite in every application's TLS config so behaviour is predictable
Centralise key operations behind an abstraction (KMS or PKCS#11) and reference keys by identifier, not algorithm
Increase RSA key length to 4096 bits across the estate
Ship private keys inside each application container so rotation is independent
questions.explanation: Crypto-agility means applications call a key by identifier ("signing-key-prod") through a KMS or PKCS#11 abstraction; the algorithm behind that identifier can be swapped from RSA to ML-KEM/ML-DSA with no application code change. Pinning a suite blocks future migration, larger RSA keys do not address Shor's-algorithm exposure, and embedding private keys in containers makes rotation harder and widens blast radius.

questions.question: During threat modelling of a new payments microservice, the team is using STRIDE. A reviewer flags that an attacker who tampers with a message between the API gateway and the ledger could silently rewrite the amount. Which control category most directly addresses this STRIDE element?
options: Rate limiting at the gateway to throttle abuse
Message-level signing (e.g., HMAC or JWS) verified by the ledger
TLS 1.3 between gateway and ledger only
Output encoding on the customer-facing API
questions.explanation: STRIDE's T is Tampering; the canonical mitigation is integrity at the message layer — HMAC or JWS — verified end-to-end so even a compromised intermediary cannot rewrite the amount. TLS 1.3 only protects the transport hop and trusts every node in the chain, rate limiting addresses denial-of-service rather than integrity, and output encoding mitigates XSS at the browser edge, not server-to-server tampering.

questions.question: A regulator now requires the firm to produce a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) for every shipped artefact and to respond to new CVEs within 72 hours. Which pipeline change most efficiently meets both obligations?
options: Generate a CycloneDX SBOM at build time, store it with the artefact, and re-scan stored SBOMs continuously against an updated vulnerability feed
Have each application team run a manual `pip list` quarterly and email the result to compliance
Block all open-source dependencies and rewrite functionality in-house
Replace SCA tooling with a network IDS to detect exploitation after release
questions.explanation: A build-time CycloneDX (or SPDX) SBOM gives a fixed inventory tied to each artefact; continuously re-scanning that stored SBOM against an updated CVE feed surfaces new vulnerabilities without needing to rebuild, which is exactly what a 72-hour response window demands. Manual quarterly lists cannot meet a 72-hour SLA, banning open-source is operationally infeasible, and an IDS detects exploitation after the fact rather than identifying vulnerable components.

questions.question: A bank is re-issuing its internal PKI. Auditors require that the root CA's private key cannot be exported, even by administrators, and that any signing event is independently logged. Which design satisfies both constraints?
options: Generate the root key in a FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM, keep it offline, and require dual-control ceremony with tamper-evident logs
Store the root key in a password-protected PFX file on an air-gapped laptop accessed by a single admin
Hold the root key in the same online subordinate CA database so issuance is automated
Encrypt the root key with the domain administrator's AD credentials
questions.explanation: A FIPS 140-3 Level 3 HSM keeps the private key non-exportable in hardware, and the documented key ceremony with M-of-N quorum plus tamper-evident logs provides the independent record auditors expect. A PFX file is exportable by anyone holding the passphrase, co-locating the root with the subordinate negates the offline-root model, and tying the key to a single AD account creates a personal single point of failure with no separation of duties.

questions.question: The SOC is buried in low-fidelity SIEM alerts and wants to bring mean-time-to-respond down without hiring more analysts. Which capability most directly addresses the volume problem?
options: A SOAR platform that runs enrichment and containment playbooks against SIEM cases
A second SIEM running in parallel for cross-validation
Switching the EDR vendor to one with a different alert taxonomy
Outsourcing the SOC entirely to a managed provider
questions.explanation: SOAR is the layer designed to triage and contain SIEM cases automatically: it enriches with threat intel, executes containment playbooks (disable account, isolate host) and only escalates the residual to a human. Running two SIEMs doubles work without reducing it, swapping EDR taxonomies does not reduce alert volume, and outsourcing transfers the problem but does not solve fidelity.

questions.question: During a tabletop, the IR lead notes that the firm's BC/DR plan promises a four-hour RTO but the database is asynchronously replicated to the DR region with a 30-minute lag. Which gap does this most directly create?
options: An RPO larger than the business has actually accepted
A bandwidth ceiling on the production link
A failure of the change-management process
A breakdown of dual-control on backup tapes
questions.explanation: RTO is how fast you can be back; RPO is how much data you can afford to lose. A 30-minute async lag locks the firm into at least a 30-minute RPO regardless of how quickly DR is brought up, so the gap is between the business's accepted data-loss tolerance and what the architecture actually delivers. Bandwidth, change-management and dual-control may all need work but are not what this specific lag exposes.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor proposes inline access to customer email for spam classification. The CISO must approve based on the firm's data-classification policy. Which control combination is the minimum acceptable safeguard for processing data marked Confidential?
options: A signed contract clause stating the vendor will "act reasonably" with the data
A signed DPA, tenant-scoped encryption keys held by the customer (BYOK), and a SOC 2 Type II report covering the relevant criteria
A vendor self-attestation that they are ISO 9001 certified
A network firewall rule restricting the vendor's source IPs
questions.explanation: For Confidential processing the firm needs contractual coverage (DPA), key control so the vendor cannot read data without the firm's key (BYOK / customer-managed keys), and independent assurance that the vendor's controls actually operate — a SOC 2 Type II covering Security/Confidentiality. "Act reasonably" is unenforceable, ISO 9001 is a quality standard with no security scope, and a firewall rule does nothing about what the vendor does with the data once it arrives.

questions.question: An architect is designing a Zero Trust deployment for a hybrid workforce. Which signal source should drive continuous access decisions, in addition to user identity?
options: Device posture (compliance, EDR health, patch level) evaluated at each request
The user's office floor number recorded in HR
Whether the user is connected to the corporate Wi-Fi SSID
The colour of the badge issued at hiring
questions.explanation: Zero Trust replaces the network-perimeter assumption with continuous evaluation of identity plus device posture — is the endpoint compliant, is EDR healthy, are patches current — re-checked at each request rather than at login. SSID and HR floor data are network/location proxies that Zero Trust explicitly distrusts, and badge colour is not a runtime authorisation signal.

questions.question: A DLP rollout keeps blocking legitimate finance traffic because executives mail spreadsheets containing what the engine classifies as PAN-like strings. Which tuning step preserves protection while reducing false positives?
options: Disable the DLP module for the finance department
Combine the regex with a Luhn check and require a second proximity keyword (e.g., "card", "CVV") before flagging
Lower the DLP confidence threshold so more events fire
Move the DLP enforcement point downstream of the mail relay so it sees fewer messages
questions.explanation: Validated detectors layer a Luhn check (real PANs satisfy the checksum, random 16-digit numbers do not) and a proximity keyword to cut the false positives without lowering protection. Disabling DLP for finance throws the policy away exactly where the sensitive data lives, lowering the threshold makes false positives worse, and moving enforcement downstream just changes when the same noise arrives.

questions.question: An attacker exploits an SSRF in a public web app to reach the cloud instance metadata service and steal a long-lived IAM role credential. Which preventive control would have most directly blocked the credential theft?
options: Disable IPv6 on the workload subnet
Enforce IMDSv2 (session-token-required metadata) so the SSRF cannot read role credentials with a simple GET
Apply a rate limit on the application's egress
Run weekly password rotation on the root account
questions.explanation: IMDSv2 requires a PUT to obtain a short-lived session token before any metadata GET succeeds; a typical SSRF that only issues GETs cannot satisfy that handshake and so cannot fetch the role credentials. Disabling IPv6 does not affect the IPv4 link-local metadata endpoint, egress rate limiting does not stop a single small request, and rotating the root password is unrelated to instance-role credential exposure.

questions.question: Forensic responders arrive at a compromised Linux host that is still powered on. Which collection order best preserves evidentiary value?
options: Pull the power cable first, then image the disk
Capture volatile memory and network state first (RAM, /proc, netstat), then a forensic disk image, then power down
Run anti-virus to clean the host before any imaging so the system is safe to keep online
Reboot into single-user mode and copy /var/log out
questions.explanation: RFC 3227's order-of-volatility says capture the most ephemeral data first: RAM, running processes, open sockets, then non-volatile disk imaging, then shut down. Pulling power destroys volatile evidence, running AV alters timestamps and may delete attacker artefacts, and rebooting clears RAM and may trigger anti-forensics in init scripts.

questions.question: A security architect must design authentication for a zero-trust network. A user's device passed posture checks at login, but the architect wants access decisions to reflect changing risk during the session. Which capability BEST supports this?
options: A longer session timeout so users re-authenticate less often.
A single strong password rotated every 90 days.
Continuous adaptive access that re-evaluates device posture, user behavior, and context throughout the session.
Static network ACLs applied only at the perimeter.
questions.explanation: Zero trust treats trust as dynamic, so continuous adaptive access re-scores signals (device posture, behavior, location, risk) during the session and can step-up authentication or cut access when risk rises. Longer timeouts weaken security, a rotated password is a one-time factor with no continuous evaluation, and perimeter ACLs contradict the zero-trust premise of no implicit trust inside the network.

questions.question: An organization is preparing for the migration risk posed by future quantum computers to its long-lived encrypted archives. Which action MOST directly addresses the 'harvest now, decrypt later' threat?
options: Increase the RSA key size to 1024 bits.
Disable TLS entirely on the archive servers.
Switch all hashing from SHA-256 to MD5 for speed.
Begin adopting post-quantum (quantum-resistant) algorithms and establish crypto-agility for data that must stay confidential for many years.
questions.explanation: 'Harvest now, decrypt later' means adversaries capture ciphertext today to break it once quantum computers mature, so data with long confidentiality lifetimes should move to quantum-resistant algorithms, backed by crypto-agility to swap algorithms as standards finalize. RSA-1024 is weaker than current norms (and still quantum-vulnerable), MD5 is broken, and disabling TLS removes protection entirely.

questions.question: A DevSecOps team wants to catch insecure code before it is merged, with minimal false-positive fatigue for developers. Which combination fits BEST in the pipeline?
options: Only run a full manual penetration test once a year.
Rely solely on end users to report vulnerabilities after release.
Integrate SAST and dependency (SCA) scanning into the pull-request pipeline with tuned rules, backed by periodic DAST on running builds.
Scan production servers weekly and skip pre-merge checks.
questions.explanation: Shifting security left means running static analysis (SAST) and software-composition analysis on every pull request with tuned rulesets to limit noise, complemented by dynamic testing (DAST) against running builds — catching issues before merge without overwhelming developers. Annual pen tests, user-reported bugs, and production-only scanning all detect problems far too late.

questions.question: An enterprise adopts a Secure Access Service Edge (SASE) model. What is the primary architectural benefit compared with backhauling all remote traffic to a central data-center firewall?
options: It eliminates the need for any identity verification.
It removes the need to encrypt any traffic.
It stores all user passwords in plaintext for faster access.
It converges network and security services in the cloud at the edge, enforcing policy close to users and reducing latency from backhaul.
questions.explanation: SASE combines networking (SD-WAN) and security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, FWaaS) as cloud-delivered services at the edge, so policy is enforced near the user rather than after hauling traffic to a central firewall — cutting latency and simplifying remote access. It strengthens (not removes) identity verification and encryption, and never implies storing plaintext credentials.

questions.question: A merger requires connecting two companies' networks quickly while limiting the blast radius if one side is compromised. Which design principle should the architect prioritize?
options: Flatten both networks into one broadcast domain for simplicity.
Share a single domain-admin account across both companies.
Segmentation with least-privilege interconnects and inspected, policy-controlled trust boundaries between the two environments.
Disable logging during the integration to reduce overhead.
questions.explanation: Segmentation with tightly-scoped, inspected interconnects contains a compromise on either side and enforces least privilege across the new trust boundary — the right principle for merging networks. Flattening into one domain maximizes blast radius, sharing a domain-admin account is a catastrophic single point of compromise, and disabling logging removes exactly the visibility a risky integration needs.

questions.question: An incident responder must preserve evidence from a running Linux server suspected of compromise, prioritizing volatile data. Following the order of volatility, which should be collected FIRST?
options: The full disk image of the system drive.
Backup tapes stored offsite.
Archived logs already shipped to the SIEM last month.
CPU registers, cache, and RAM contents (including running processes and network connections).
questions.explanation: The order of volatility dictates capturing the most ephemeral data first — CPU registers/cache and RAM (with live processes and connections) vanish on power-off, so they are collected before the disk image. Disk images are less volatile, and already-archived SIEM logs or offsite tapes are the least volatile and can be gathered later.

questions.question: A company deploys an API gateway in front of dozens of microservices. Which control at the gateway MOST directly mitigates abuse from a compromised or malicious client flooding requests?
options: Returning verbose stack traces so clients can self-diagnose.
Allowing unlimited requests but logging them for later review.
Rate limiting and throttling per client/identity, combined with authentication and quota enforcement.
Disabling TLS to reduce handshake overhead under load.
questions.explanation: Per-client rate limiting, throttling, and quota enforcement at the gateway blunt request floods and abuse while authentication ties limits to identity — the core availability/abuse control for APIs. Verbose stack traces leak information, log-only with unlimited requests does nothing to stop the flood in real time, and disabling TLS trades away confidentiality and integrity for a marginal performance gain.

questions.question: A regulated firm must prove that cryptographic keys used to sign transactions cannot be extracted by administrators. Which control BEST provides this assurance?
options: Store the keys in a spreadsheet protected by a strong password.
Keep the keys in application source code under version control.
Email the keys to a second administrator as a backup.
Generate and use the keys inside a FIPS 140-2/3 validated hardware security module (HSM) so private keys never leave the device in plaintext.
questions.explanation: An HSM generates and uses private keys inside tamper-resistant, validated hardware and never exports them in plaintext, so even administrators cannot extract them — the strong assurance a regulated signing workflow needs. Spreadsheets, emailed copies, and keys committed to source control all expose the private key material directly.

questions.question: A threat-intelligence program wants to move from reacting to alerts toward anticipating adversary behavior. Which practice BEST supports proactive defense?
options: Waiting for antivirus signatures to be updated by the vendor.
Blocking only the specific file hashes seen in the last incident.
Mapping observed and expected adversary techniques to a framework such as MITRE ATT&CK to drive detections and threat hunting.
Turning off alerts that fire too often to reduce workload.
questions.explanation: Mapping adversary behavior to MITRE ATT&CK lets a team reason about techniques (not just indicators), build behavior-based detections, and hunt proactively for activity that has not yet triggered an alert. Waiting on signatures and blocking single hashes are reactive and easily evaded, and silencing noisy alerts risks hiding real activity rather than improving defense.

questions.question: An architect must protect sensitive data used by analysts who need to run queries but should never see raw personally identifiable information (PII). Which technique BEST enables analysis while protecting the PII?
options: Grant analysts full read access and trust them not to misuse it.
Encrypt the database and share the decryption key with all analysts.
Delete all PII so no analysis is possible.
Apply data tokenization or format-preserving masking so analysts work with de-identified values while referential integrity is preserved.
questions.explanation: Tokenization or format-preserving masking replaces PII with de-identified surrogates that keep the data usable for joins and analysis without revealing the underlying values — enabling analytics while protecting the sensitive fields. Trusting full access defeats the control, deleting all PII destroys needed context, and sharing the decryption key with everyone effectively exposes the plaintext.
